extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in literary theory and narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining Bakhtin's concept of heteroglossia and how multiple voices, registers, and discourses operate within language and the novel; useful as guidance for analyzing or employing dialogic/multi-voiced techniques in creative writing and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteroglossia (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heteroglossia is the coexistence of distinct linguistic varieties, styles of discourse, or points of view within a single language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term translates Russian raznorechie and was introduced by Mikhail Bakhtin; frames language as containing multiple 'languages' or voices within one language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties as points of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence in language of a variety of 'points of view on the world, forms for conceptualizing the world in words, specific world views, each characterized by its own objects, meanings and values.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stratifications represent distinct perspectives; they are not merely lexical differences but different ways of evaluating and conceptualizing social reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of context over text
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word uttered, in any specific time or place, is a function of a complex convergence of forces and conditions unique to that time and place; the primacy of context over text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heteroglossia is 'the base condition governing the operation of meaning in any utterance' — meaning arises from situated, contextualized use rather than abstracted system rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language is not a finished system
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is never a finished, ordered system: it is a work in progress, always ongoing, never complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bakhtin rejects treating language as an abstract system; attempts to systematize language reify a posited ideal and ignore the living, disordered reality of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrifugal vs centripetal forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between centrifugal (dis-ordering, diverse, decentralizing) forces and centripetal (unifying, ordering) forces in language and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centripetal forces are reflected in standardisation, grammar rules, dictionaries and linguistics; centrifugal forces are disparate, plural, and produce heteroglot reality. Writers and analysts should recognise both kinds of pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language stratifies into many voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Any language stratifies into many voices: 'social dialects, characteristic group behaviour, professional jargons, generic languages, languages of generations and age groups, tendentious languages, languages of the authorities, of various circles and of passing fashions'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bakhtin asserts this diversity of voice is the defining characteristic of the novel; incorporation of these stratifications produces richness and social verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: No neutral words / words bear speaker signature
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are 'shot through with intentions and accents' and there are no neutral words; even ordinary statements bear the 'signature of the speaker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words acquire social flavor and are tied to groups, professions, times and places; analysts should avoid assuming lexical neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogized heteroglossia
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogized heteroglossia refers to the relations and interactions between these languages within an individual speaker; the languages 'interanimate' one another as they enter into dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one person may use Church Slavonic to God, family dialect with kin, songs in another tongue, official high-class diction for petitions — these registers interact rather than remain compartmentalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: A hybrid utterance is a passage using a single speaker but different kinds of speech, where juxtaposition brings contradiction and conflict in belief systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique often used for parody or irony (e.g., Dickens shifting from narrative to epic/formal tone); concealed speech without markers enables authorial parody and refracted authorial intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Authoritative discourse demands assimilation by the reader/listener; it is viewed as past, finished, hierarchically superior and 'demands unconditional allegiance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discourse is not open to interpretation and thus 'plays an insignificant role in the novel' because novels function by questioning authoritative positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the novel: to promote heteroglossia
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of the novel is to draw the authoritative into question and to allow what was once considered certain to be debated and open to interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novels should incorporate multiple voices and perspectives; failing to do so is characterized as an artistic failure by Bakhtin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic features as traces of social attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic features are not fixed and definitive but are 'traces', 'crystallizations', or 'sclerotic deposits' of attitudes and worldviews resulting from forms of active participation in life and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features reflect social experience and changing participation; critics should read features as social evidence rather than as immutable rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice guideline for prose writers
rubrics_metrics.description: The prose writer must welcome and incorporate these many languages into their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should deliberately include stratified voices, registers and jargons to reflect social heteroglossia and to produce dialogic depth in narrative voice.
